title: Blues as secular spirituals; hearing blues in Philadelphia
summary: He says the blues belongs to nobody and was only captured by Handy, and recalls corner guitarists and Baltimore's role in music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Oh, a lot of our things that we did, like the Blues was just a secular form of the spirituals. Or when -- anything like that. And like blues, "I Hate to See the Evenin' Sun Go Down", that don't belong to nobody. The man that captured it was W.C. Handy, but it didn't belong to Handy.
It's just the blues. And then when the great singers come along in the age later on, like Bessie Smith, Ethel Waters, and all of them, they sang blues.
When did you first hear -- had you heard blues at this point in Philadelphia?

Oh, yes. Oh, yeah, you heard that with the guitars. The guy would stand on the corner and they'd be selling oysters or something like that. Or there'd be a blind man playing that, you know, we'd filled a pepper pot. And most of the guys were like from Baltimore. That was Eubie Blake's home, Baltimore. And Chick Webb's home was Baltimore. A lot of the musicians and all. But Baltimore was a great center for music, too.. Philadelphia was. Philadelphia piano players. Baltimore give you guitars, and tenor banjoes and banjoes, at the time.
